title: Who, which and that
summary: Using the ligatures -ng, -g and na to say the child who is eating, the house which was burned, the food that was cooked
goals: See how a ligature does the job of English who, which and that
Join a noun and a verb in either order: ang batàng kumakain or ang kumakaing batà
Read and build sentences such as Maliít ang sapátos na binilí ko
Link a person's name to a verb, preferring na: Si Pedro na umáawit

sections.title: Ligatures as who, which and that

blocks.t: English uses **relative pronouns** such as *who*, *which* and *that* to connect a description to a noun that comes before it: *the child **who** is eating*.

Tagalog does the same job with a **ligature** (**-ng**, **-g** and **na**). The ligature connects a noun or pronoun to a **verb** (or the verb to the noun), and the result is a phrase that works like a relative pronoun. The rules for choosing the ligature are the ones from **Lesson 7** (Words that Link and Describe).

blocks.title: Ligature rules from Lesson 7
items: Word ends in a **vowel**: add **-ng** (batà → batà**ng**).
Word ends in another **consonant**: use **na** as a separate word (báhay **na**).

blocks.t: As in Lesson 7, **changing the order** of the noun (or pronoun) and the verb **does not change the meaning**.

head: Noun first
Verb first
Meaning
blocks.title: The ligature stands for who, which, that

items.tl: Ang súlat na tinanggáp ko ay kanyá.
items.en: The letter that I received was his/hers.

items.tl: Maliít ang sapátos na binilí ko.
items.en: The shoes that I bought were small.
We who are studying are being disturbed by you. (literal)
The women who are singing are beautiful.

items.tl: Ang laláking natútulog ay ginígising ng batà.
items.en: The man who is sleeping is being awakened by the child.

items.tl: Ang mga tinátawag mo ay iyóng mga umáalis.
items.en: The ones that you are calling are those who are leaving.

blocks.title: Who, which and that in sentences
Find the ligature
blocks.t: In each sentence, look for the **-ng** or **na** that joins a noun or pronoun to a verb: súlat **na** tinanggáp, sapátos **na** binilí, kamí**ng** nag-áaral, babáe**ng** umáawit, laláki**ng** natútulog, iyó**ng** mga umáalis. That ligature is the English *who / which / that*.
When the subject is a **person's name**, it is not wrong to attach **-ng** or **-g** to the name:

items.tl: Si Pedrong umáawit ay kaibígan ko.
items.en: Pedro, the one who sings, is my friend.

items.tl: Si Juang sumulat nitong kuwento ay may sakít.
items.en: Juan, the (one) who wrote this story, is sick.

blocks.t: However, using the ligature **na** after a person's name is **more common**:

items.tl: Si Pedro na umáawit ay kaibígan ko.
items.en: Pedro, the one who sings, is my friend. (same meaning as Si Pedrong umáawit…)

items.tl: Si Juan na sumulat nito ay may sakít.
items.en: Juan, the (one) who wrote this, is sick. (same meaning as Si Juang sumulat…)

blocks.title: More common: na after a name
Remember
items: A ligature (-ng, -g, na) joining a noun and a verb = who, which or that.
Choose the ligature with the Lesson 7 rules: vowel → -ng, n → -g, other consonant → na.
Noun first or verb first, the meaning is the same: ang báhay na nasúnog = ang nasúnog na báhay.
After a person's name, na is more common: Si Pedro na umáawit.

exercises.q: In this lesson, what does the job of English who, which and that?
exercises.explain: The ligature joins the noun or pronoun to the verb.

exercises.q: Which means the same as "ang báhay na nasúnog"?
exercises.explain: Changing the order does not change the meaning.

exercises.q: Which means the same as "ang pagkaing nilutò"?
exercises.explain: Nilutò ends in a vowel, so it takes -ng.
Báhay ends in a consonant (y), so na is used.

exercises.q: Join kumakain and batà, verb first (the child who is eating).
exercises.explain: Kumakain ends in n, so add -g.

exercises.q: Fill in: Maliít ang sapátos ___ binilí ko.
exercises.explain: Sapátos ends in s, so na is used.

exercises.q: "Ang súlat na tinanggáp ko ay kanyá" means…
options: The letter that I received was his/hers.
The letter that I wrote was his/hers.
exercises.answer: The letter that I received was his/hers.

options: The women who are singing are beautiful.
exercises.answer: The women who are singing are beautiful.

exercises.q: "Ang laláking natútulog ay ginígising ng batà" means…
options: The man who is sleeping is being awakened by the child.
The child who is sleeping is being awakened by the man.
The man is waking the child.
exercises.answer: The man who is sleeping is being awakened by the child.

exercises.q: Which is more common after a person's name?
exercises.explain: Si Pedrong umáawit is not wrong, but na is more common.

options: We who are studying are being disturbed by you.
You are studying and we disturb you.
exercises.answer: We who are studying are being disturbed by you.

exercises.explain: From the book's exercise: the dress which she will wear (isusuót).

exercises.q: Which ligature is joined to Juan in "Si Juang sumulat…"?
exercises.explain: Juan ends in n, so -g is added.

recap: A ligature (-ng, -g, na) joining a noun or pronoun and a verb works like who, which or that.
Use the Lesson 7 rules: vowel → -ng, n → -g, other consonant → na.
The order can swap without changing the meaning: ang batàng kumakain = ang kumakaing batà.
Maliít ang sapátos na binilí ko. The shoes that I bought were small.
After a name, -ng/-g is not wrong, but na is more common: Si Pedro na umáawit ay kaibígan ko.
